title: Colours, Images and Sound
summary: A colour is three numbers - red, green and blue light, usually 0 to 255 each. An image is a grid of those colours, and compression makes it smaller. Sound is the air pressure measured tens of thousands of times a second, each measurement a number.
markdown:
## Colour: three numbers A screen makes every colour by mixing three lights: **red, green and blue** (RGB). Each is a number, usually from **0 to 255** (one byte): | Colour | Red | Green | Blue | Hex | |---|---|---|---|---| | Black | 0 | 0 | 0 | `#000000` | | White | 255 | 255 | 255 | `#FFFFFF` | | Red | 255 | 0 | 0 | `#FF0000` | | Yellow (red + green light) | 255 | 255 | 0 | `#FFFF00` | | Orange | 255 | 136 | 0 | `#FF8800` | | Mid grey | 128 | 128 | 128 | `#808080` | Three bytes per colour is **24 bits**: 256 × 256 × 256 = **16,777,216** colours. The hex form you see in web pages and design tools is just the three bytes in a row: `#FF8800` is FF (255) red, 88 (136) green, 00 blue. Light mixes differently from paint: red and green **light** make yellow, and all three at full make white. Often there is a fourth byte, **alpha**, for how see-through a pixel is: RGBA, 32 bits per pixel. ## Images: a grid of colours An image is a grid of pixels, each one colour. Size is easy to work out: > 1920 × 1080 pixels × 3 bytes = **6,220,800 bytes**, about 6 MB, for one uncompressed full-HD picture. A phone photo of 12 million pixels would be 36 MB that way, yet the file is about 3 MB. That is **compression**: | Kind | How | Examples | Good for | |---|---|---|---| | **Lossless** | Finds repetition and stores it more briefly ("200 white pixels" instead of 200 copies). Decompresses to exactly the original | PNG, GIF, ZIP | Screenshots, diagrams, text, anything with sharp edges | | **Lossy** | Throws away detail the eye barely notices | JPEG, WebP, and video: H.264, AV1 | Photos and video, where files become 10 to 100 times smaller | A video is a series of images, typically 24 to 60 per second, compressed by also storing mostly what **changes** between frames. ## Sound: measuring the air Sound is the air pressure wobbling back and forth. A microphone turns it into a changing voltage, and the computer **samples** it: measures it many times a second and stores each measurement as a number. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Air pressure wave"] --> M["Microphone
voltage"] --> C["Converter samples it
44,100 times a second"] --> N["Numbers:
0, 2034, 3871, 5102, ..."] ``` | Setting | CD audio | Meaning | |---|---|---| | Sample rate | 44,100 per second | Must be over twice the highest pitch people hear (about 20,000 Hz) | | Bits per sample | 16 | Each measurement is a number from −32,768 to 32,767 | | Channels | 2 | Left and right | One second of CD audio: 44,100 × 2 bytes × 2 channels = **176,400 bytes**. A 3-minute song is about 32 MB uncompressed, and about 3 MB as MP3 or AAC, which are lossy formats that drop sounds people cannot hear well. To play sound, the computer sends the numbers back to a converter that turns them into a voltage, which moves a speaker, which moves the air. ## Everything is numbers Text (3.01), fractions (3.03), colours, pictures, sound: each is turned into numbers by an agreed rule, and the numbers into bits. Whatever a computer seems to work with, underneath it is working with numbers, and the program is what remembers what they mean. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What colour is #00FF00? - Red + Bright green - Blue > Red 00, green FF (255), blue 00. ? How many bytes does an uncompressed 100 × 100 RGB image take? - 100 - 10,000 + 30,000 > 100 × 100 pixels × 3 bytes. ? What is the difference between lossless and lossy compression? - Lossy files are always bigger - Only lossless works on photos + Only lossless gives back the exact original > Lossy compression throws away detail people barely notice, to save more space. PNG is lossless; JPEG is lossy. ? Why is CD audio sampled 44,100 times a second? - That is how fast CD players spin + It is over twice the highest pitch we hear - It is the largest 16-bit number > The sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency. People hear up to about 20,000 Hz, so the rate needs to be over 40,000. ```

Bright green

Red 00, green FF (255), blue 00.

cards.q: How many bytes does an uncompressed 100 × 100 RGB image take?
What is the difference between lossless and lossy compression?
cards.a:
Only lossless gives back the exact original

Lossy compression throws away detail people barely notice, to save more space. PNG is lossless; JPEG is lossy.

cards.q: Why is CD audio sampled 44,100 times a second?
cards.a:
It is over twice the highest pitch we hear

The sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency. People hear up to about 20,000 Hz, so the rate needs to be over 40,000.
